## 3. Management Following Diagnosis

### 3.1. Initial risk stratification

The clinical course of acute PE is highly heterogeneous, with mortality risk influenced by the hemodynamic consequences of the thrombotic burden and by patient factors such as physiological reserve [[19](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib19)]. Consequently, several attempts have been made to identify clinical signs or symptoms that allow for reliable, standardized risk stratification.

The most immediate determinant of an adverse outcome is hemodynamic instability, typically defined as persistent hypotension with a systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg for at least 15 minutes. In an analysis of 15 520 patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE) from the RIETE registry, Laporte et al. [[20](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib20)] found hemodynamic instability to be the strongest independent predictor of mortality, with an odds ratio (OR) of 18.6 compared with patients without symptomatic PE, substantially exceeding conventional risk factors such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, or advanced age. Accordingly, 10 guidelines define high-risk PE as the presence of hemodynamic instability [[[6]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6), [[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)].

In most patients, however, PE does not result in hemodynamic instability but may still exert strain on the right ventricle due to increased afterload. A 2023 meta-analysis of 63 studies reported a pooled risk ratio of 3.77 (95% CI, 1.61-8.80) for PE-related death in patients with echocardiographic signs of right ventricular abnormalities, albeit with a low positive predictive value (9%; 95% CI, 6%-12%) and not stratifying for vital parameters [[21](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib21)]. While echocardiography offers real-time bedside assessment of right ventricular performance, it may not be universally available. In such cases, computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), already the diagnostic standard for PE, can provide evidence of right ventricular abnormalities, such as an increased right-to-left ventricular ratio. A 2015 meta-analysis of 49 studies, including 13 162 patients, found that right ventricular dilation on CTPA (defined as a ratio ≥ 1.0) was associated with an OR of 5.0 (95% CI, 2.7-9.2) for PE-related death [[22](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib22)]. Although both modalities reliably detect right ventricular abnormalities, they assess different aspects of ventricular function: CTPA primarily structural, and echocardiography functional. Current evidence does not support a preference for one modality over the other; rather, it highlights their complementary roles in comprehensive risk assessment of acute PE.

The increase in right ventricular afterload may also cause myocardial injury, as measured by elevated cardiac biomarkers, most commonly troponin. In a 2019 meta-analysis of 46 studies, elevated troponin was associated with an OR of 4.33 (95% CI, 3.27-5.74) for mortality [[23](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib23)].

The prognostic importance of right ventricular abnormalities and myocardial injury is widely recognized. Ten guidelines recommend routine imaging (echocardiography or CTPA) for right ventricular assessment [[[6]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6), [[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)], and 9 recommend troponin testing in normotensive patients [[[6]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6), [[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. However, because the direct consequences of these findings have not been proven in prospective management studies, their integration into risk categories is not uniform. Five guidelines classify any patient with either right ventricular abnormalities or troponin elevation as intermediate risk [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)], whereas 4 advocate further subclassification: patients with both risk factors are considered intermediate-high risk, for whom close hemodynamic monitoring and parenteral anticoagulation for the first 2 to 3 days are suggested [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15)]. In support of this notion, the ESC/ERS highlight the results of the influential 2014 PEITHO trial, in which the time from diagnosis to hemodynamic decompensation or death in 499 patients with both right ventricular abnormalities and elevated cardiac biomarkers was 1.79 ± 1.60 days [[24](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib24)].

A subset of hemodynamically stable patients might be characterized as sufficiently low risk of deterioration to warrant home treatment without initial hospital admission [[[25]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib25), [[26]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib26), [[27]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib27)]. To aid in their identification, guidelines recommend 1 of 3 validated prognostic tools. The PE Severity Index (PESI) was introduced by Aujesky et al. [[28](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib28)] in 2005, based on a retrospective sample of 10 354 patients. The 5-tier approach, comprising 11 clinical variables, categorizes patients into five 30-day mortality risk classes ([Supplementary material](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#appsec1)) and has subsequently been validated in American and European cohorts [[28](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib28),[29](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib29)]. In response to its complexity, a simplified PESI (sPESI) was introduced in 2010, reducing the number of variables to 6 and classifying risk dichotomously ([Supplementary material](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#appsec1)) [[30](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib30)]. A 2016 meta-analysis showed that both scores accurately predicted 30-day mortality, with rates of 2.3% (95% CI, 1.7%-2.9%) for PESI and 1.5% (95% CI, 0.9%-2.5%) for sPESI in low-risk patients [[31](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib31)]. Eight guidelines endorse the use of PESI or sPESI for identifying low-risk candidates for outpatient management [[5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib5),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)].

However, it is important to note that sPESI may not be sufficient on its own to guide decisions regarding outpatient treatment. The 2021 randomized HOME-PE trial demonstrated that although sPESI was safe in identifying patients eligible for home treatment, nearly one-third of patients with a score of 0 were not treated at home due to medical or social considerations identified by the treating physician [[26](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib26)].

The Hestia criteria, aptly named after the Greek goddess of domestic life, provide an alternative approach. Unlike sPESI, Hestia includes social and logistical considerations, such as family support and the ability to adhere to therapy, alongside clinical markers ([Supplementary material](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#appsec1)). In the 2011 derivation study, Zondag et al. [[32](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib32)] reported on a Dutch cohort of 297 patients who met the Hestia criteria and were discharged within 24 hours for home treatment with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). The 3-month recurrence rate of VTE was 2.0% (95% CI, 0.8%-4.3%), major bleeding 0.7% (95% CI, 0.08%-2.4%), and mortality 1.0% (95% CI, 0.2%-2.9%), with no deaths attributable to PE. Subsequent studies in European and North American populations have confirmed these findings [[26](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib26),[33](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib33)]. Accordingly, all but 4 guidelines (THANZ, AHA, JCS, and IUA) actively recommend the use of the PESI, sPESI, or Hestia criteria [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib5),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)].

With respect to home treatment, there is broad consensus: 10 guidelines support outpatient care for patients deemed low risk and with adequate home support [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib5),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. One notable caveat is UpToDate, which recommends the exclusion of residual deep vein thrombosis before outpatient management, citing its association with early adverse events, but without providing evidence from outcome trials to substantiate this recommendation [[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17),[34](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib34)].

In summary, most guidelines acknowledge that risk stratification should be conducted immediately following PE diagnosis and used to guide subsequent management. Indeed, all guidelines, except the IUA, recommend that management following diagnosis be based on stratification into groups according to expected mortality [[[4]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4), [[5]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib5), [[6]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6), [[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[12]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12), [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. The most widely recommended method is endorsed by 7 guidelines and encompasses the assessment of hemodynamic instability, right ventricular abnormalities, cardiac biomarkers, and clinical scoring tools for prognostic evaluation, such as the Hestia criteria and the PESI or sPESI score [[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)].

Based on clinical assessment, 5 guidelines recommend stratifying patients into high-, intermediate-, and low-risk groups [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)], whereas 4 further subcategorize intermediate-risk into intermediate-high and intermediate-low to better inform monitoring and treatment intensity [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15)].

### 3.2. Anticoagulation therapy

Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of treatment for acute PE, aiming to prevent thrombus propagation and reduce the risk of recurrence. While anticoagulants do not directly dissolve the embolism, they attenuate further clot formation by inhibiting the coagulation cascade. Further, by reducing thrombin generation, they also decrease activation of the thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor, thereby indirectly enhancing plasmin activity and promoting endogenous fibrinolysis [[35](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib35)].

Historically, initial treatment consisted of intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH), a parenteral anticoagulant that binds to antithrombin III, inducing a conformational change that increases its inhibition of thrombin and factor (F)Xa [[36](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib36)]. Heparin has the advantage of an immediate onset and a titratable effect, reaching peak activity within hours of administration. The introduction of VKAs in the 1950s marked a major therapeutic advance by enabling long-term oral anticoagulation [[37](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib37)]. VKAs function by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, thereby blocking the activation of clotting FII, FVII, FIX, and FX. Due to their delayed onset, requiring several days to achieve a therapeutic effect, VKAs must be initiated concurrently with a parenteral agent, such as heparin, until stable anticoagulation is achieved.

The subsequent advent of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), including rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran, has significantly reshaped contemporary guidelines due to their efficacy, safety, and ease of administration. These agents target specific components of the coagulation cascade: rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban inhibit FXa, while dabigatran inhibits thrombin (FIIa).

Rivaroxaban was the first DOAC approved for the treatment of VTE following the pivotal EINSTEIN-PE trial in 2012 [[38](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib38)]. In this randomized trial of 4832 patients, rivaroxaban demonstrated noninferiority to standard therapy (low-molecular-weight heparin [LMWH] followed by VKA) in terms of recurrent VTE (hazard ratio [HR], 1.12; 95% CI, 0.75-1.68; _P_ = .003 for noninferiority) and was associated with a significantly lower rate of major bleeding (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.31-0.79; _P_ = .003). The AMPLIFY trial, published the following year, evaluated apixaban in 5395 patients with PE or deep vein thrombosis, demonstrating similar noninferiority for recurrence or VTE-related death (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.60-1.18; _P_< .001) and a substantially lower risk of major bleeding (RR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.17-0.55; _P_< .001) [[39](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib39)].

These findings have had a substantial impact on clinical guidelines. Rivaroxaban and apixaban are now recommended as first-line therapy by 11 [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11),[[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)] and 10 [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11),[13](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)] guidelines, respectively. The lower frequency of apixaban recommendations primarily reflects the earlier publication date of the SPAIN guideline, which preceded EMA approval of apixaban. In comparison, edoxaban and dabigatran are both endorsed by 7 guidelines [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7), [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib8), [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14)]. In the 2013 HOKUSAI-VTE trial, edoxaban was shown to be noninferior to warfarin for the prevention of recurrent VTE (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.70-1.13; _P_< .001), although it did not demonstrate superiority in bleeding outcomes (HR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.59-1.21; _P_ = .35) [[40](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib40)]. Similarly, dabigatran was shown to be noninferior to warfarin in the 2014 RE-COVER II trial (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.76-1.57), with a comparable bleeding profile (HR for major bleeding, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.48-1.11) [[41](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib41)].

Although DOACs have been in clinical use for over a decade, comparative data between individual agents remain limited. A 2019 meta-analysis by Aryal et al. [[42](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib42)] pooled data from 5 observational studies comprising more than 45 000 patients and found no significant difference in recurrence risk between apixaban and rivaroxaban, but apixaban was associated with a lower risk of major bleeding (RR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.58-0.93) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (RR, 0.59; 95% CI, 0.50-0.70). Recent observational evidence further supports the favorable bleeding profile of apixaban. In a North American population-based cohort study of 163 593 patients with VTE between 2016 and 2024, apixaban was associated with a lower risk of recurrent VTE (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78-0.96) and major bleeding (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.63-0.75) compared with rivaroxaban [[43](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib43)]. Similarly, in a Swedish nationwide registry of 19 090 cancer-free patients aged ≥65 years with VTE between 2014 and 2023, rivaroxaban was associated with a higher risk of major bleeding compared with apixaban during the initial 6 months of treatment (adjusted HR [aHR], 1.46; 95% CI, 1.15-1.85), albeit with no difference when treatment was extended beyond 6 months (aHR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.94-1.63) or in the incidence of recurrent PE (aHR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.47-1.04) [[44](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib44)]. The ongoing COBRRA and DANNOAC-VTE trials (NCT03266783 and NCT03129555, respectively) are expected to provide further prospective evidence on bleeding outcomes between these 2 agents [[45](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib45),[46](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib46)].

Overall, most guidelines recommend DOACs over VKA-based regimens in patients with low- to intermediate-risk PE, citing favorable safety and efficacy profiles. However, 6 guidelines specify that in patients at high risk of hemodynamic deterioration, UFH or LMWH should be preferred due to their rapid onset of action and widely available antidote [[[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. When choosing among DOACs, guidelines generally emphasize the individualization of therapy based on anticipated adherence, renal function, cost, and availability. A recurring rationale for the preference of rivaroxaban and apixaban is their single-drug regimen, avoiding the initial LMWH bridging required by edoxaban and dabigatran, a distinction reflected in the THANZ guideline, which notes, “oral factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., apixaban, rivaroxaban) are preferred…because they do not require parenteral anticoagulation for initiation” [[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16)].

In addition to general recommendations for the broader population, several guidelines also provide guidance on anticoagulation in challenging subgroups, such as those with active cancer, renal impairment, or antiphospholipid syndrome. For example, in patients with malignancy, some guidelines favor DOACs while others recommend LMWH as first-line therapy, particularly in the setting of gastrointestinal cancer. In renal failure, UFH and dose-adjusted LMWH are generally preferred due to their predictable pharmacokinetics and reversibility. Similarly, VKAs remain the anticoagulant of choice in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome. However, there is substantial variation in these recommendations across guidelines, reflecting both the complexity of clinical decision-making and the limitations of available trial data. A comparison of guideline recommendations regarding special populations, as well as cases of right heart thrombi and subsegmental emboli, is beyond the scope of this review but can be found in the Supplementary material.

The duration of anticoagulation remains a key area of variability. Ten guidelines recommend a minimum primary treatment course of 3 months, regardless of provoking factors [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11), [[12]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12), [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13),[[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. However, recommendations on extended therapy differ substantially. In cases of unprovoked PE, active malignancy, or hemodynamic severity, guideline recommendations range from 3 to 12 months, underscoring the need to weigh thrombotic vs bleeding risk on a case-by-case basis [[47](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib47)].

### 3.3. Thrombolytic therapy

In contrast to anticoagulants, thrombolytic agents directly lyse existing emboli by catalyzing the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, thereby promoting fibrin degradation. Given its potential to rapidly restore pulmonary perfusion, reduce right ventricular afterload, and prevent circulatory collapse, systemic thrombolysis, typically administered as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, plays a central role in the treatment of high-risk PE, albeit at the cost of increased bleeding risk.

The most comprehensive analysis comparing thrombolysis with anticoagulation alone was conducted by Marti et al. [[48](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib48)] in a 2014 meta-analysis of 2057 patients across 15 trials. In the subset of 4 trials enrolling patients with hemodynamic instability, thrombolysis significantly reduced PE-related mortality (OR, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.03-0.78). However, overall mortality did not differ significantly (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.20-1.15), primarily due to an increased incidence of major bleeding in the thrombolysis group (9.9% vs 3.6%). Notably, the risk of major bleeding varied by thrombolytic agent, with alteplase showing a more favorable profile (OR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.43-2.62) compared with tenecteplase (OR, 5.02; 95% CI, 2.72-9.26), although this difference attenuated in sensitivity analyses excluding 1 alteplase trial with a more restrictive bleeding definition [[49](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib49)].

To date, the only study directly comparing thrombolysis with anticoagulation in high-risk PE is a 1995 randomized trial by Jerjes-Sanchez et al. [[50](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib50)]. In this trial, terminated early after enrolling 8 patients, those randomized to receive streptokinase and UFH had 100% survival, while all patients receiving UFH alone died within hours of presentation [[50](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib50)].

The convincing reduction in PE-related death among high-risk patients is reflected in the guidelines, which all 11 address the use of thrombolytics, supporting its use in this population under careful consideration of bleeding risk and the feasibility of alternative reperfusion strategies, such as catheter-directed intervention or surgical embolectomy [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[12]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12), [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. An overview of absolute and relative contraindications to thrombolysis, as specified by each guideline, is provided in the Supplementary material.

In intermediate-risk PE, however, the role of thrombolysis remains contentious. These patients are hemodynamically stable but exhibit right ventricular abnormalities and/or myocardial injury. The landmark 2014 PEITHO trial investigated this population, randomizing 1005 patients with both right ventricular abnormalities and elevated troponin to receive either tenecteplase plus UFH or placebo plus UFH [[24](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib24)]. Thrombolysis significantly reduced the composite endpoint of death or hemodynamic decompensation within 7 days (OR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.23-0.87), but at the cost of increased extracranial bleeding (OR, 5.55; 95% CI, 2.30-13.39) and stroke (OR, 12.10; 95% CI, 1.57-93.39). Importantly, there was no significant difference in serious adverse events by day 30 (OR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.62-1.34).

In light of these findings, 8 guidelines offer conditional support for thrombolysis in intermediate-risk patients, particularly those with a high likelihood of deterioration or a low bleeding risk [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. For example, the 2020 ASH guideline recommends considering thrombolysis in selected young patients with a low hemorrhagic risk [[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7)]. Conversely, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, GSA, and ESC/ERS explicitly advise against thrombolysis in hemodynamically stable patients, regardless of evidence of right ventricular strain [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[13](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13)]. Instead, they advocate for close clinical surveillance and early escalation in cases of deterioration. Interpretation of these recommendations is complicated by the heterogeneity in risk stratification frameworks. Five guidelines define intermediate-risk PE as the presence of either right ventricular abnormalities or elevated cardiac biomarkers [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)], while 4 apply a stricter definition, reserving the label of intermediate-high risk for patients with both findings [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15)]. These inconsistencies likely influence downstream recommendations and contribute to the variation in guideline positions.

In summary, current guidelines support the use of thrombolysis in high-risk PE with hemodynamic instability. In intermediate-risk PE, guidelines differ considerably. The general consensus is that thrombolytic therapy is indicated in the setting of treatment failure, determined on a case-by-case basis. Multidisciplinary evaluation remains essential to balance the competing risks of hemodynamic collapse and iatrogenic harm.

### 3.4. Mechanical and surgical intervention

Although systemic thrombolysis remains the primary reperfusion strategy in patients with high-risk PE, it is contraindicated in cases of major bleeding risk, including recent neurosurgical intervention or central nervous system neoplasia. In such scenarios, catheter-directed and surgical interventions offer alternative approaches to reduce thrombotic burden and alleviate right ventricular strain.

Catheter-directed therapies encompass a range of minimally invasive techniques, including mechanical fragmentation, aspiration thrombectomy, and low-dose catheter-directed thrombolysis. These procedures are performed via percutaneous access and allow localized intervention within the pulmonary vasculature. Conversely, surgical embolectomy involves direct thrombus extraction under cardiopulmonary bypass, generally via a longitudinal incision of the pulmonary arteries.

Eight clinical guidelines recommend catheter-directed intervention for patients with high-risk PE in whom systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or if clinical deterioration persists despite thrombolytic therapy [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. Although randomized evidence is limited, observational studies have demonstrated promising outcomes. One of the most cited is the 2015 SEATTLE II trial, a prospective single-arm study of 150 patients with proximal PE and a right-to-left ventricular ratio ≥ 0.9 on CTPA [[51](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib51)]. Of these, 31 patients were classified as high risk due to shock, syncope, or recent cardiac arrest. Instead of systemic thrombolysis, treatment consisted of ultrasound-assisted, catheter-directed, low-dose thrombolysis (24 mg of tissue plasminogen activator), which resulted in a mean reduction in the right-to-left ventricular ratio of −0.51 and in pulmonary artery systolic pressure of −12.6 mm Hg, improvements similar to those observed in the 119 patients with intermediate-risk PE. However, high-risk patients exhibited a higher incidence of major bleeding compared with intermediate-risk patients (23% vs 7%; _P_ = .02).

More recently, the FLAME study evaluated outcomes in 53 high-risk patients treated with the FlowTriever system (Inari Medical), a mechanical thrombectomy device that uses aspiration catheters and nitinol mesh discs [[52](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib52)]. The nonrandomized study reported an all-cause mortality of 1.9% (95% CI, 0.0%-10.1%), markedly below the prespecified performance goal of 28.5% derived from a contemporaneous meta-analysis [[53](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib53)]. Rates of major bleeding (11.3%; 95% CI, 4.3%-23.0%) were comparable to the performance goal of 11.5%. When interpreting these data, it should be noted that patients were enrolled at the discretion of the investigators, suggesting selection bias, and that results from ongoing randomized controlled trials are necessary to substantiate these findings.

In patients with intermediate-risk PE, catheter-directed interventions are endorsed by 4 guidelines as potential alternatives to systemic thrombolysis, particularly in cases of deteriorating clinical status or relative contraindications to thrombolytic agents [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16)]. Ongoing randomized trials are expected to inform future recommendations [[[54]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib54), [[55]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib55), [[56]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib56), [[57]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib57), [[58]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib58), [[59]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib59), [[60]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib60)].

In contrast to catheter-based modalities, surgical embolectomy is currently reserved for high-risk patients in whom thrombolysis has failed or is contraindicated. Of the 8 guidelines addressing surgical management, 7 recommend surgical embolectomy only in rescue settings [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)], whereas the THANZ guideline allows earlier use based on institutional expertise [[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16)].

A 2021 scientific statement by the AHA reviewed 12 retrospective studies, including 836 patients, and reported in-hospital mortality rates ranging from 2.3% to 13.2%, depending on preoperative resuscitation status [[61](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib61)]. Contemporary techniques involve direct pulmonary artery incision and thrombus extraction, often accompanied by intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography for guidance [[62](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib62),[63](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib63)].

Despite these improvements, no randomized or comparative studies on surgical embolectomy have been published. While interest has increasingly focused on less invasive catheter-based approaches, surgical embolectomy remains an essential option, particularly for patients with intracardiac thrombi. Future trials are needed to clarify its role and guide its integration into treatment algorithms.

In select cases of profound circulatory collapse, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been proposed as a bridge to definitive catheter-based or surgical treatment. In this regard, recommendations for ECMO are present in 4 guidelines. The ESC/ERS states that ECMO may be considered in combination with surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy in patients with refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9)]. Similarly, the PE Response Team Consortium and UpToDate endorse ECMO as a potential supportive intervention for patients undergoing reperfusion therapy or awaiting surgical intervention [[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. The JCS guideline recommends ECMO consideration for cardiogenic shock when conventional treatments fail [[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12)]. Despite these endorsements, robust comparative data are lacking, and ECMO use remains limited to specialized centers with relevant expertise.

Overall, both catheter-based and surgical interventions are recognized by most guidelines as critical components of the therapeutic arsenal for acute PE in patients with contraindications to thrombolysis or who deteriorate despite adequate treatment. While these modalities and the potential addition of ECMO are increasingly incorporated into guideline frameworks, the general consensus is that their application should be based on a comprehensive evaluation of patient risk, bleeding profile, and institutional capabilities.

### 3.5. Supportive treatment

While anticoagulation and reperfusion therapies remain the primary strategies for managing PE, supportive measures offer aid in stabilizing patients, particularly those at high risk of hemodynamic deterioration. In this regard, contemporary guidelines offer recommendations on fluid treatment, oxygen supplementation, vasopressor or inotropic support, and, in selected cases, the placement of inferior vena cava filters.

The purpose of inferior vena cava filters is to prevent embolization of residual thrombus from the deep venous system into the pulmonary arteries, potentially aggravating the vascular obstruction. Their use is generally reserved for patients in whom anticoagulation is contraindicated or for those with recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation. Eleven [[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib4),[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib7),[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11), [[12]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12), [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13), [[14]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib14), [[15]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15), [[16]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib16), [[17]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)] and 6 [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9), [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10), [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib11), [[12]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12), [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib13)] guidelines endorse the use of inferior vena cava filters under these conditions, respectively. Notably, the indications for their placement have narrowed over time; for instance, the 2011 AHA guideline also adds poor cardiopulmonary reserve and large free-floating proximal thrombi as potential indications, and the 2009 JCS guideline endorses placement in cases requiring thrombolysis or intrapelvic thrombosis [[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib6),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12)]. Overall, guidelines consistently discourage the routine use of filters due to the risk of thrombosis and the lack of mortality benefit in controlled trials and meta-analyses [[64](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib64),[65](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib65)].

Fluid treatment in acute PE requires careful consideration. Although hypotension may suggest a need for volume expansion, excessive fluid administration can exacerbate right ventricular dysfunction by increasing wall stress and impairing left ventricular filling. Despite a paucity of direct evidence for PE, 5 guidelines provide specific recommendations. UpToDate, GSA, ESC/ERS, and SPAIN advise cautious volume administration, typically ≤500 mL of isotonic saline, preferably guided by clinical assessment or passive leg raise [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. In contrast, the JCS guideline advises against fluid loading, citing the potential for worsening right ventricular overload, and instead advocates for early vasopressor support [[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12)].

Oxygen therapy is considered the mainstay in the treatment of hypoxic patients; however, as hypoxemia in PE is a consequence of a mismatch between ventilation and perfusion, it should be kept in mind that normoxemia can only be attained through simultaneous pulmonary reperfusion. The lack of robust evidence on the optimal approach in this setting is reflected by the included guidelines, of which 5 actively provide recommendations; UpToDate, GSA, ESC/ERS, JCS, and SPAIN suggest initiating supplementary oxygen when the arterial oxygen saturation falls below 90% to 92%, with acceptable thresholds ranging from >90% to 96% [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. The ESC/ERS further recommends high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation in cases of impending cardiac arrest, citing a 2017 correspondence in which 17 intensive care unit patients achieved a significant increase in oxygen saturation from 93% to 100% (_P_< .001) by means of a high-flow nasal cannula with FiO2 settings at 1.0 and flow at 60 L/min [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[66](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib66)]. The JCS further advises intubation if oxygen saturation cannot be maintained above 90% with conventional oxygen therapy, but cautions against the possible detrimental effects of increased intrathoracic pressure [[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12)].

Recent studies have further explored the physiological effects of oxygen therapy in nonhypoxemic PE. The AIR trial, a randomized study of 70 patients with intermediate-risk PE, found that supplemental oxygen resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the right-to-left ventricular ratio compared with ambient air (0.28 vs 0.12; _P_ = .02), suggesting a potential role in alleviating right ventricular afterload despite normoxaemia [[67](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib67)]. Complementing these findings, the SO-PE trial is currently investigating the effects of oxygen on pulmonary vasodilation and right ventricle-pulmonary artery coupling using advanced echocardiography and metabolomics in nonhypoxemic PE patients with right ventricular abnormalities [[68](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib68)].

In patients with massive PE and hypotension or shock, the use of vasopressor and inotropic therapy has been considered in 5 guidelines. The preferred agent in this setting is the vasopressor noradrenaline, as recommended by UpToDate, GSA, SPAIN, and JCS in cases of hypotension, whereas the ESC/ERS recommends its use only in cardiogenic shock [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib12),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15),[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib17)]. Among inotropic agents, dobutamine is generally favored by guidelines, with the GSA, ESC/ERS, and SPAIN recommending its use in instances of low cardiac output but sustained systemic pressures [[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib9),[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib10),[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib15)].

Together, these supportive strategies provide essential adjuncts to definitive therapy in acute PE. While largely extrapolated from physiological principles and observational data, their integration into clinical guidelines underscores the importance of individualized management, particularly for patients with high-risk or complex presentations.

### 3.6. Future directions

Despite substantial advances in the management of acute PE, several clinically important questions remain unresolved. The optimal selection of patients for catheter-directed therapies, including the identification of subgroups most likely to benefit and the standardization of procedural endpoints, warrants further prospective evaluation. Similarly, a consensus definition of treatment failure, for instance, based on clinical deterioration or lack of improvement, would strengthen comparability across future trials. The appropriate dose and duration of anticoagulation remain under investigation, as evidenced by the recent Hi-Pro and RENOVE trials, which explore reduced-dose regimens and individualized treatment durations to balance efficacy against bleeding risk [[69](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib69),[70](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783625009006#bib70)]. Another important area of uncertainty is the management and follow-up of patients in whom PE is discovered incidentally, for whom the optimal intensity and duration of therapy remain undefined. Collectively, these gaps highlight the need for large, harmonized clinical studies to refine treatment algorithms and guide management across the full spectrum of PE severity.

## 4. Conclusion

This review provides an overview of the 14 most recent guidelines on the treatment of acute PE and highlights important recent literature. A common approach across guidelines involves initial risk stratification into high-, intermediate-, or low-mortality risk based on hemodynamic status, right ventricular abnormalities, cardiac troponin levels, and prognostic scoring tools such as sPESI.

Most guidelines agree that patients at high risk, typically characterized by persistent hypotension, are candidates for immediate thrombolysis and heparin. In cases of contraindications or treatment failure, catheter-directed or surgical interventions are commonly considered. For intermediate-risk patients, most guidelines favor the initiation of rivaroxaban or apixaban, with treatment durations ranging from 3 to 12 months, depending on recurrence risk. In patients showing clinical signs of deterioration, parenteral anticoagulation may be preferred, and some guidelines support considering thrombolysis. In low-risk patients, DOACs are generally endorsed, and outpatient management is considered appropriate when supported by tools such as the Hestia criteria.

In summary, the key conclusion is that while international guidelines converge on the general treatment pathway, from anticoagulation to risk-adapted reperfusion, important discrepancies remain regarding intermediate-risk management, optimal treatment duration, and supportive care. Harmonization of these recommendations through future prospective and comparative studies is essential to ensure consistent, evidence-based management of PE worldwide.

 Lung disease (e.g., any cause of hypoxemia and/or hypercapnia). (28024557)
  + ARDS
    - ~25% of patients with ARDS may have RV dysfunction. (29744563)
    - Risk factors for RV dysfunction include:
    - (1) Severe hypoxemia (e.g., PaO2/FiO2 < 150).
    - (2) Hypercapnia (e.g., PaCO2 > 48 mm).
    - (3) High airway pressures.
    - (4) Pneumonia.(33853435, 29744563)
  + Pneumonia.
  + Lung overdistension: excessive PEEP or autoPEEP.
  + Lung underdistention: atelectasis, pleural effusion, pneumothorax.
  + Sickle cell acute chest syndrome (~20% incidence of RV failure).(29744563) [...] This is unknown, but some considerations include the following:
 MAP > (60 mm + CVP). 
  + Patients with markedly elevated CVP might need a higher MAP target to achieve adequate systemic perfusion pressures. Such patients may benefit from a combination of simultaneous vasoconstrictors plus diuresis (to promote decongestion and optimize right ventricular preload). When in doubt, it may be reasonable to trial an elevated MAP to see whether it improves urine output. Once the patient is adequately decongested, you can often wean off vasoconstrictors (“squeeze and diurese” strategy).
  + A recent retrospective trial found benefit from a dynamic MAP target of (60 + CVP) in a group of patients with precapillary pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. (37817916)

# [Internet Book of Critical Care (IBCC)](https://emcrit.org/)
